title: Claude, Codex, and Hermes installed unowned code inside corporate networks
gist: Israeli security researchers found 120 of 8,265 scanned llms.txt/llms-full.txt files across 6,214 corporate domains pointed to unregistered software packages or domains, and coding agents (including Claude, OpenAI's Codex, and Nous Research's Hermes) at dozens of Fortune 500 companies automatically installed and executed the researchers' proof-of-concept payloads — revealing a new large-scale supply-chain attack surface created by AI agents trusting vendor-published 'AI-readable' documentation.

themes.theme: New attack surface: llms.txt supply-chain risk

insights.claim: Researchers scanned 6,214 live domains belonging to defense contractors, Fortune 500s, and Big Tech firms, finding 8,265 llms.txt/llms-full.txt files, of which 120 (each on a different site) pointed to unregistered code packages or domain names.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the vulnerability: roughly 1.5% of scanned llms.txt files across a sample skewed toward the largest, best-resourced companies contained exploitable dangling references — a measurable, scannable supply-chain risk category.

insights.claim: The 120 misconfigured files contained 227 total commands referencing non-existent packages or unclaimed domains, meaning each vulnerable file often had multiple exploitable references.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Confirms the issue is systemic rather than a handful of isolated typos, suggesting broad remediation work will be needed across the corporate web as llms.txt adoption grows.

insights.claim: When researchers registered a handful of the unclaimed package/domain names referenced in these files and set up beacons, they received phone-home responses within an hour from a Fortune 500 company, followed by a few dozen more responses from other Fortune 500 firms and startups over time.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Empirically proves the vulnerability is being actively (if unintentionally) exploited in the wild by production AI coding agents inside real corporate networks, not just a theoretical risk — a live incident-response-worthy finding.
insights.quote: Within an hour, the researchers received a phone-home response from a Fortune 500 company.

insights.claim: The beacon's process-chain logging revealed that coding agents including Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's Codex, and Nous Research's Hermes were the parent processes that triggered the unauthorized package installs; Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nous Research did not respond to requests for comment.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Names the specific commercial AI coding agents implicated, which is directly material to any assessment of agentic coding-tool safety and vendor liability exposure for Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nous Research.

insights.claim: At least one active real-world attack was found exploiting this exact mechanism: the legitimate site clerk.com hosted an llms.txt instructing 'npx clerk-next-fix-auth-protection,' and an attacker had already claimed the once-empty npm slot to host live malware before Clerk resolved the issue.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Moves the threat from theoretical PoC to confirmed live exploitation in production, meaning any company with an outdated or auto-generated llms.txt file faces genuine near-term malware risk via its own AI-assisted developer tooling.
insights.quote: The researchers soon discovered that someone had claimed the once-empty slot and used it to host live malware.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'As the researchers' PoC demonstrates'

themes.theme: The broken trust model between AI agents and documentation

insights.claim: The core failure mechanism is that AI coding agents treat any vendor-published, HTTPS-hosted, standardized-format documentation file as inherently authoritative, without verifying that referenced packages exist in the actual registry namespace or that referenced domains are still owned by the claimed party.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural, not incidental, flaw in how current agentic coding tools establish trust — a systemic risk that will recur across any 'AI-readable' documentation convention unless agent vendors add verification layers.
insights.quote: The agent has no reason to question any of it. The file is the authority—that's its entire purpose.
insights.locator: section 'The collapsing boundary between data and code'

insights.claim: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools and corporate proxies see nothing anomalous in these attacks because the traffic pattern looks exactly like a legitimate developer running pip/npm install from an allowed domain (pypi.org, npmjs.org) via a company-sanctioned coding agent as the parent process.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Explains why traditional enterprise security tooling (EDR, proxy allowlists) is structurally blind to this class of attack, implying current corporate security stacks need new controls specifically for agentic-AI-driven package installation.
insights.quote: To any EDR or proxy, this looks like a developer running a legitimate package manager: pip install from pypi.org—a domain every corporate proxy already allows.
insights.locator: section 'The collapsing boundary between data and code'

insights.claim: Trust in these documentation files is transitive across a supply chain: an agent that trusts a partner or vendor's documentation will follow that trust even if the compromised reference sits several hops away from the ultimate target company (e.g., a partner's docs or a community project's setup guide).
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Multiplies the attack surface well beyond a single company's own documentation, since any AI agent trusting a third-party vendor/partner inherits that party's llms.txt risk — relevant to enterprise third-party risk management frameworks.
insights.quote: The trust chain is transitive, too.
insights.locator: section 'The collapsing boundary between data and code'

insights.claim: Researcher Alon Hertz distinguishes this vulnerability from classic prompt injection: no malicious actor needs to plant anything at the time the instruction is written, since a completely benign real company document becomes dangerous only later, when the referenced package or domain is abandoned and claimed by an attacker.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: This 'time-delayed, ownerless' exploit pattern is broader and harder to defend against than conventional prompt injection because it requires no compromise of the original source — meaning static content audits alone won't catch it; ongoing registry monitoring is needed.
insights.quote: Here, the instruction itself can be completely benign and come from a legitimate source—a real company's own documentation—with no malicious actor involved at the time it was written. The danger comes later, when the package or domain it points to is abandoned and someone else claims it.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning '"The Clerk case is the cleanest proof of it"'

insights.claim: Researchers found that many of the faulty package/domain references in llms.txt files predate the AI era, having originated in earlier non-LLM documentation files, indicating human error (not just AI hallucination) is also a major source of these dangling references.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Suggests remediation must include auditing legacy documentation, not just newly AI-generated content, broadening the scope of any cleanup effort companies undertake.

insights.claim: The researchers argue that LLMs' fundamental inability to distinguish trusted user instructions from untrusted third-party content is the same root cause behind conventional prompt injection, but this newly identified vulnerability class is broader because it applies to any content an agent processes, not just deliberately crafted attacks.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Frames this as a fundamental, currently 'unsolvable' architectural limitation of LLM agents rather than a patchable bug — a meaningful risk factor for the broader thesis that agentic AI can be safely given broad execution permissions in enterprise environments.
insights.quote: This so-far unsolvable shortcoming causes prompt injections.
